implementation_notes: The smallest C++ realization: one std::future per subtask, aggregation by calling get() as each future becomes ready. The launch policy must be passed explicitly - the default (async | deferred) lets the implementation defer the call to the first wait, silently serialising the work on the caller's thread. std::async with launch::async is specified to run as if in a new thread, so it is a thread-per-subtask form: cap the number of live futures (a sliding window of in-flight tasks) when the subtask count is large, or move to a pool.
pitfalls: std::async without an explicit std::launch::async may run deferred, so the fan-out quietly becomes sequential.
One thread per subtask oversubscribes when the subtask count far exceeds the core count; keep the in-flight window bounded.
A throwing subtask rethrows from f.get(); collect results per future so one failure does not discard the other partials.

variants.name: Hand-built worker pool over a mutex/condition-variable queue
variants.idiom_name: std::thread pool + std::deque task queue + std::condition_variable
variants.implementation_notes: The classic POSA structure written directly: a fixed set of std::thread workers pops std::function tasks from a std::deque guarded by std::mutex, waiting on a std::condition_variable; a poison pill (empty function or a stop flag) terminates the loop, std::thread::join is the barrier and the master aggregates the per-task results afterwards. Choose it when dispatch policy matters - task priority, batching, per-queue affinity, or a worker count the standard library does not let you control - and remember it is not work stealing.
pitfalls: wait must use the predicate overload and the queue must be re-checked after every wakeup, or workers pop an empty queue.
Destroying the pool while workers are still blocked in wait is undefined; the stop signal must be pushed and joined before members are destroyed.
A single queue serialises dispatch under the mutex; at high task rates use per-worker queues or a lock-free queue and accept reordering.

variants.name: oneTBB task_group over a work-stealing arena (C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: oneTBB owns a work-stealing pool: task_group::run submits a subtask, wait() is the join and run_and_wait returns a value, while parallel_for/blocked_range covers regular data decomposition and the task_arena (or global_control) bounds the worker count. Choose it when the pool must be sized, tasks must nest (a worker spawning more work without deadlocking) or the standard library's thread-per-subtask behaviour is too expensive; the cost is an external dependency and a build-system change.
pitfalls: Push into a shared container from parallel tasks needs its own synchronisation or a concurrent container.
A task must not block on another task's result: use task_group/flow-graph dependencies, because blocking a worker can deadlock the arena when it holds the work the dependency needs.
